sn52.8:1.1: Salaḷa was the awakening tree of the Buddha Paduma (Tha Ap 179:1.2), which suggests it was a large tree. It is sometimes identified with frankincense (sallakī, Sanskrit śallakī, Boswellia serrata), but seems to me unlikely. Frankincense thrives in arid highlands quite distant from the rich riverlands of Sāvatthī, and is a straggly tree unsuited to construction (although the hut could simply be near a frankincense). The flowers or garlands of salaḷa are, in poetry, abundant (eg. Ja 511:27.3, Tha Ap 209, Tha Ap 556:3.3), but the frankincense flower is small and a poor candidate for garlands. MN 93:11.6 and MN 96:16.3 speak of the fire of the salaḷa, but no Pali reference, so far as I know, speaks of the most characteristic feature of frankincense, its aromatic gum used for incense. Sometimes the variant readings suggest a confusion with the pine tree sarala (Pinus roxburghii, SN 56.32:2.2), but that of course has no flowers.
